newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: Ex-beauty queen plans Venezuelan presidential bid.
newsitem.headline: Ex-beauty queen plans Venezuelan presidential bid.

text.p: Irene Saez, a former Miss Universe and Venezuela's most popular politician, is preparing to announce a bid for president next year.

"I know the moment will come to announce it and take a firm decision," the 34-year-old Saez told Reuters in an interview late on Monday. "I want to wait until next year and in the meantime prepare the path."

Saez is Venezuela's leading political phenomenon. Her statuesque figure and billowing blonde hair bring her instant recognition and her standing in the polls -- at more than 50 percent -- is more than double that of her closest rival.

"People are waiting for a political leader, a messiah ... and I'm realising that people are pointing to me," Saez said in the clearest indication yet that the woman who won the Miss Universe title in 1981 and is currently mayor of Caracas district Chacao has set her sights on the country's top job.

Re-elected in 1995 for a second three-year term as mayor with more than 90 percent of the vote, Saez was quick to stress that she was virtually being carried to the presidential palace on a tide of public opinion.

"I never proposed that I should be president ... It's something amazing that people are queuing and queuing to say that Irene Saez should run for president, that she should run as an independent, that we believe in her."

While voters may at first have been influenced by her good looks and fame, her popularity has been buttressed by the remarkable success of her Chacao administration. Critics who ridiculed the idea of a beauty queen turned politician have had to swallow their words.

Crime has been slashed by a well-equipped and educated police force, traffic laws -- routinely flouted in the anarchic capital of 5 million people -- are strictly enforced, and a budget deficit has been turned into surplus.

Her unparalleled voter appeal has created major headaches for Venezuela's traditional political parties. One of the oldest and largest, the social Christian party Copei, recently changed its statutes, paving the way for a possible Saez candidacy on a Copei ticket.
Still, many political analysts have dubbed her a "Barbie doll" with a fuzzy political platform. Critics say her popularity would evaporate if she left Chacao, which is known locally as "Irenelandia."
But Saez is not intimidated. "We've had nearly 40 years experience of people who know everything ... and look at the results."
Her experience as an 18-year-old Miss Universe was ideal preparation for a political career, she said. "It helped me to know how to compete. The competition between women is very, very tough."
Nor does Saez feel the male-dominated world of Venezuelan politics would refuse to accept a female president.

"Our country has always been in the hands of men ... so why not give a woman a chance?" she asked, adding that female candidates were expected to run in upcoming elections in Ecuador, Colombia and Bolivia.
